identity.title: Procedural Pretraining: Warming Up Language Models with Abstract Data

problem.claim: The paper studies whether exposing language models first to abstract, procedurally generated structured data can ease later acquisition of semantic knowledge compared with direct web-scale pretraining.

contributions.claim: It diagnoses which algorithmic skills different procedural-data forms can improve and reports substantial gains for several skills.
It studies procedural-data front-loading in models up to 1.3B parameters, including performance, data-use, and FLOP-related outcomes.
It explores benefits through attention and MLP structure and proposes combining multiple procedural-data forms.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors present procedural pretraining as a simple, lightweight approach that separates aspects of knowledge acquisition from reasoning in language-model pretraining.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that context-recall accuracy on a Needle-in-a-Haystack task rises from 10% to 98% after pretraining on Dyck sequences.
The authors report that front-loading 0.1–0.3% procedural data significantly outperforms standard natural-language pretraining on C4, CodeParrot, and DeepMind-Math datasets.
The authors report reaching the same loss using 55%, 67%, and 86% of the original data, with a comparable reduction in FLOPs.

narrative_sequence.summary: The paper contrasts direct web-scale pretraining with an alternative inspired by learning simple formal structures before higher reasoning.
It uses procedural data generated by formal languages and simple algorithms as abstract structured data.
It first links procedural-data types to algorithmic skills, then evaluates front-loading at scales up to 1.3B parameters and reports gains, data savings, and FLOP reductions.
It examines structure in attention and MLP layers, differentiates their reported relevance across domains, and outlines combining procedural-data forms.

source_observation.claim: The abstract pairs skill-specific diagnosis with downstream pretraining results and then relates the gains to distinct structures in attention and MLP layers.

lessons.interpretation: A staged account can connect what a data intervention improves, where it transfers, and what internal mechanism may explain the transfer.
lessons.application: For a new pretraining intervention, organize evaluation from targeted capability diagnostics to downstream benchmarks and a mechanism analysis tied to the observed domain differences.
lessons.exception: This sequence may be unsuitable when the intervention has no separable target capability or when internal measurements cannot support a meaningful mechanism claim.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify model architectures, training schedules, baseline configurations, statistical variability, or the exact meaning of the three reported data-retention percentages.
The reported mechanism findings and performance comparisons are author-reported; the abstract does not provide enough detail to assess causal attribution or reproducibility.
